items.title: A thousand slogans echoed here - but it could be the end for iconic Delhi protest site
items.summary: Jantar Mantar, an 18th Century site almost synonymous with demonstrations in Delhi, has been denotified as a protest site.
items.content:
To raise your voice against injustice? To draw attention to a cause? Or to make those in power uncomfortable enough to listen?

For more than three decades, Indians have tried to do all three in a narrow, tree-lined road near Jantar Mantar, an 18th Century astronomical obervatory in Delhi.

This week, Delhi Police said Jantar Mantar, located close to parliament, would no longer be a designated protest site.

The decision comes months after the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - not a political party but a collective which began as a joke - led a massive protest there demanding the resignation of federal education minister Dharmendra Pradhan. Tens of thousands turned up and Pradhan subsequently resigned.

Police barricaded Jantar Mantar soon afterwards, preventing further demonstrations. Last week, an attempt by CJP supporters to march there, this time demanding the resignation of India's election chief, ended in a police crackdown .

Protesters have now been directed to three other sites. Two are far from parliament, while the third, the sprawling Ramlila Ground, is often booked months in advance. Unlike Jantar Mantar, which is free, all three charge tens of thousands of rupees a day.

Delhi Police says , external it acted after the Supreme Court suggested identifying alternative sites with adequate infrastructure. But critics say the move could push protests beyond the reach of ordinary Indians, further from the seat of power and into venues many cannot afford.

Over the years, Jantar Mantar has witnessed everything from mass movements that shook governments to small, lonely demonstrations by people desperate to be heard. Farmers, students, grieving parents and ex-soldiers have gathered under its trees, holding placards and shouting slogans. Not every protest made headlines, but for many, it was a place to turn to when other doors had closed.

This week, when the BBC visited, those scenes seemed a distant memory.

Yellow barricades blocked both ends of the road, with hundreds of paramilitary personnel standing guard, batons in hand.

In a nearby lane, uniformed men sat in shops drinking tea or scrolling through their phones. At one of the few shops without policemen, the shopkeeper folded his hands and said he did not want to answer any questions.

Built by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II in the 1720s, Jantar Mantar was once better known as a tourist attraction than a place where a thousand revolutions were imagined.

Its story as a protest site began in 1993, when the then-Congress government stopped allowing demonstrations at the Boat Club lawns opposite the old parliament.

Historian Harleen Kaur has traced how, from the 1960s onwards, successive governments brought in new rules that shifted the site of protest in Delhi further away from parliament.

"Jantar Mantar, situated 3km (1.86 miles) from the Parliament House, [allowed the government] to contain protesting crowds at some distance from the Parliament House and PM's residence," she wrote in a 2023 paper , external .

Yet, the road saw countless spirited protests over the years.

Rachna Dhingra, an activist with the Bhopal Group for Information and Action, an advocacy group for survivors of a 1984 gas leak disaster, camped at Jantar Mantar with hundreds of others for around five months in 2008, trying to get the government to agree to demands including setting up a commission to allocate resources for rehabilitation schemes.

Through a scorching summer, they held press conferences, met politicians and even chained themselves to railings opposite then Prime Minister Manmohan Singh's residence to draw attention to their cause.

It was also where she formed solidarities with others - Tibetans protesting against China, activists opposing the displacement of people over large dam projects and even just lone protesters who caught a train from their home towns with nothing but a placard and a grievance.

"It can be lonely to protest but that place became a home for so many of us. We shared each other's stories, struggles and victories," says Dhingra.

Dipa Sinha, an academic associated with the Right to Food campaign, has seen ground-breaking laws - a landmark rural jobs guarantee scheme , the National Food Safety Act and Forest Rights Act - take shape at Jantar Mantar.

"It was a place where you could discuss issues with people who came to Delhi from across the country," she says.

Protesters would demonstrate outside government offices, including the erstwhile Planning Commission and the agriculture ministry, where they were often detained by police, before returning to Jantar Mantar to "gather, discuss and strategise".

Dhingra says they sheltered under tarpaulin sheets when it rained, used public toilets near the site and went to nearby gurdwaras to freshen up.

In 2017, the National Green Tribunal cited the lack of infrastructure, along with complaints from locals, to have Jantar Mantar shut down for protests.

A year later, the Supreme Court overturned this, citing the rights to free speech and peaceful assembly guaranteed under the constitution.

When asked whether the proximity to parliament made a difference to their cause, Dhingra quoted the reactions of her co-protesters who had come to Delhi for the first time.

"That's the president's house? Does the prime minister live there? How can they not listen to us when we are at their gates?" she remembered them saying.

Sinha points out that Jantar Mantar was also near institutions like the Press Club and Constitution Club, making it easier to get media coverage, and for politicians to drop by and meet protesters.

It was a simpler time - sometimes they would ask for permission from police only on the morning of the protest.

In recent years, when Dhingra tried to protest at Jantar Mantar, she was told no-one could stay the night.

"Where do you go with hundreds of people who have travelled all the way to the capital to protest?" she asks.

While Jantar Mantar has its supporters, others share memories of an even more vibrant protest culture.

Mary E John, a gender studies scholar who lived in Delhi both as a student and as an academic, says that before 1993, she attended protests at the Boat Club on issues ranging from workers' rights and women's issues to topics of international significance.

"We lived in a climate where protest was part of life. In fact, we took it for granted," she says.

When the spacious Boat Club lawns made way for Jantar Mantar, it actually felt "claustrophobic", she said.

She pointed out that they, and others before and after them, protested at multiple sites - universities, colleges, streets - instead of just at Jantar Mantar.

She sees signs of that in protests by farmers who camped at Delhi's borders for months, and people who sat at the Shaheen Bagh neighbourhood demanding the repeal of a controversial citizenship law.

Even the 2012 anti-rape protests, she points out, were not restricted to Jantar Mantar but almost reached the Indian president's heavily guarded complex and beyond into other parts of Delhi.

It's not clear what Jantar Mantar's future is - the Supreme Court is hearing pleas challenging its removal as a protest site.

Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and CJP leaders have said that Jantar Mantar belongs to the people and will be "reclaimed".

As the debate rages on, Jantar Mantar is the quietest it has been in decades - will it hear slogans again?

items.title: Judge throws out child sex abuse charges against actor Timothy Busfield
items.summary: The judge in the case said on Friday that the prosecutor "failed to act in a fair and impartial manner".
items.content:
A judge in the US state of New Mexico has thrown out charges against Emmy-winning actor Timothy Busfield, saying there were issues with how prosecutors presented the case.

The West Wing and Field of Dreams actor was indicted in February on four counts of criminal sexual contact of a child. Busfield has denied all the allegations.

The charges stemmed from accusations brought by child actors he worked with on the Fox series The Cleaning Lady, which he directed and produced.

The judge said on Friday that the prosecutor "failed to act in a fair and impartial manner". The district attorney's office said it was evaluating options on how to move forward.

Actor Timothy Busfield indicted on child sexual contact charges

State District Judge Joseph Montano granted the defence's motion to dismiss the indictment on Friday, citing mistakes that undermined the grand jury process.

"Our office has received the order and is evaluating our options to determine how we will proceed," a spokesperson for the Office of the Second Judicial District Attorney in Bernalillo County told the BBC on Friday.

The actor surrendered to state authorities in January when a warrant was issued for his arrest. A judge later ordered his release pending trial.

Busfield had originally been taken into custody in Albuquerque on two counts of criminal sexual contact with a minor and one count of child abuse.

The indictment against him, reviewed by the BBC, said that on or between 19 October 2022 and 10 September 2023, Busfield "touched or applied force to the intimate parts" of one of the unnamed boys when he was under the age of 13.

The Thirtysomething actor's defence team submitted more than 70 letters from people vouching for his character and said that he underwent and passed a polygraph test pertaining to the allegations against him.

In a warrant for Busfield's arrest, prosecutors had said the parents of the boys alleged that he groomed and sexually abused the youngsters while working on The Cleaning Lady.

Authorities claimed the boys referred to Busfield as "Uncle Tim" and alleged that he "would tickle them on the stomach and legs". Both boys told authorities they were touched inappropriately for years, his arrest affidavit stated.

Busfield's lawyers had said the actor was being accused as an act of revenge after the children were fired from the series, which angered their mother.

items.title: Trump 'completely wrong' to restrict support for Ukraine, Italian minister tells BBC
items.summary: Defence Minister Guido Crosetto tells the BBC the US risks prolonging Russia's full-scale invasion rather than helping to end it.
items.content:
Italy's defence minister has said it was a "complete mistake, a major mistake" for the US to limit access to satellite systems and intelligence used by Ukraine to defend itself against Russian attacks.

Guido Crosetto warned in a BBC interview that any such move by US President Donald Trump's administration "makes absolutely no sense" and risked prolonging Russia's full-scale invasion rather than helping to bring peace. Trump has denied asking for satellite access to be suspended.

Crosetto's comments continue Italy's sharpening criticism of the US.

Earlier this week, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called Trump's deal to buy diesel from Russia a "very risky choice" and said it would "grant Russia legitimacy" as it bombed cities in Ukraine.

Trump agreed the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, blaming Kyiv's own attacks on Russian refineries for rising fuel prices.

Meloni, once considered so close to the US president she was dubbed a "Trump whisperer", said the move ran counter to efforts to bring Putin to the negotiating table.

"Peace will come when Putin is convinced there is a stalemate, that he cannot advance any further," her defence minister told the BBC at his ministry building in Rome.

Crosetto was a co-founder of Meloni's hard-right Fratelli d'Italia party, which has led a right-wing government coalition since 2022, shortly after the start of Russia's full-scale war.

"If [Putin] sees weakness on the Ukrainian side – and if the US deprives Ukraine of resources, that creates weakness – then he will believe he can win. So he will continue the war," Crosetto warned.

Despite widespread public scepticism, Meloni's Italian government has been a strong ally of Ukraine from the start, sending both military and humanitarian aid.

The specifics of those deliveries have always been classified.

Crosetto said that victory for Ukraine would be "a victory for peace, a victory for justice, a victory for international law".

He vowed that Italian military support would continue "for as long as this government is in place", though he warned that getting Italy's parliament to approve further deliveries would be "more difficult" as elections approached.

The vote has to take place by the end of 2027 and opinion polls currently put a new far-right party, Futuro Nazionale, ahead of all Meloni's coalition partners.

That party's leader, former general Roberto Vannacci, is openly sympathetic to Russia and opposes aiding Ukraine, arguing that Europe is wasting its money as Russia's military "continues to advance" on the ground.

At a recent event in Tuscany, he described himself as "neither pro-Putin nor pro-Russian" but "pro-Italian".

Crosetto brushed off questions about Vannacci, including on whether his views reflected those of many Italians, saying he had more "serious matters to deal with".

But, perhaps to underline the difference, he was unequivocal on Russia.

"When one state crosses another state's border with tanks, when it bombs hospitals and schools, kills civilians and bombs power plants, and has been doing so for four years, I can only describe that as evil," he said.

Zelensky says Ukraine has right to defend itself after Trump calls latest strikes a 'disgrace'

Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back - with Starlink playing a key role

Italians, like many Europeans, are seeing prices go up, driven by the high cost of energy.

During street protests in Rome on Friday, where firecrackers were thrown, secondary school students complained that resources were being diverted to arms instead of education.

In southern Italy, truckers have begun blocking roads complaining at the hike in fuel prices.

Polls here regularly show that a majority of Italians want an end to military aid for Ukraine. One, conducted for the Ixè institute in September, put support for continuing to supply arms at just 18%.

There are many factors behind that, from a long-standing pacifist tradition to a history of strong business ties to Moscow. Unlike Poland or the Baltic states, Italy feels physically distant from the danger, too.

But the defence minister also blamed an active campaign of disinformation by Moscow – targeting, he said, "certain political figures... and narratives to weaken the political climate against Russia".

"In some way they shift public opinion," the minister argued.

"It's very hard to explain to a citizen who's having trouble at the petrol pump that we can't give any concessions to Russia right now. But that's the only way to defend the future of that very citizen who's complaining."

Italy has not been targeted for major acts of sabotage, unlike other allies of Ukraine in Europe.

The minister said a fire at an arms depot outside Rome in August was not arson, but "human stupidity".

A report last month that Russia was planning to launch drone attacks at Italy, France and Spain from the container ships in the Mediterranean was not proven, Crosetto also told us.

But cyber-attacks, which he linked to Russia, were now routine - "there are hundreds every day" - and he believed Europe had been too weak in its response.

"You can't win a war... if you don't fight back," the minister said.

items.title: Dam removals are bringing fish back across the northeastern United States
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/dam-removals-are-bringing-fish-back-across-the-northeastern-united-states-striking-down-one-tiny-barrier-at-a-time-180989679/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50126312 Points: 16 # Comments: 2
items.content:
In 1859, a committee of farmers in Billerica, Massachusetts, having grown irked by a dam on the Concord River, hired a surveyor to justify its destruction. The dam, which powered a textile factory owned by an industrialist named Charles Talbot, was allegedly flooding their fields and spoiling their hay; now they wanted the wall and its reservoir gone. They hoped the surveyor’s evidence would persuade a court to order its obliteration. The surveyor—a conscientious, lushly bearded man of good repute—set about plumbing the Concord’s bottom, measuring its bridges and scrutinizing high-water marks. In truth, he didn’t love the work, describing surveying as “drudgery” in his journals. Henry David Thoreau ’s truest passion, of course, wasn’t surveying land, but writing about it.

Aside from the paycheck, the now-legendary author had another motivation to take the Concord job: He despised the Talbot Mills Dam. A decade earlier, Thoreau had published the travelogue A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers , in which he inveighed against the dam for blocking the passage of spawning fish, especially American shad. “Poor shad! Where is thy redress?” Thoreau wrote . Although Thoreau’s surveys supported the farmers’ case, on appeal, the state of Massachusetts permitted the dam to remain. This can’t have surprised Thoreau, who knew that dams made for intractable opponents. “Perchance, after a few thousands of years, if the fishes will be patient, and pass their summers elsewhere meanwhile, nature will have leveled the Billerica dam,” he wrote.

For many fish-blocking dams, however, it hasn’t taken “a few thousands of years” to level them after all. Since 1912, more than 2,300 dams have been purged from waterways in the United States, most in the last quarter-century. The dam-removal movement hit its apogee in 2024, when, by the accounting of the nonprofit American Rivers, dam removals reconnected more than 2,500 miles of once-fragmented waterways . The year’s biggest and best-publicized dam obliteration occurred on the Klamath River, where the dismantling of four aging hydroelectric dams opened more than 400 miles of spawning habitat in California and Oregon to chinook salmon, which recolonized the watershed so rapidly that conservationists described the comeback as “ magical .” Before the Klamath, the nation’s largest undamming took place on Washington State’s Elwha River, where two fish-blocking walls were obliterated on behalf of chinook, coho, steelhead and other salmonids.

Yet it would be a mistake to presume that dam removals primarily benefit western salmon rivers. Though they’re typically smaller in scale and receive less fanfare, the majority occur in eastern states. In 2024, the Blake Higgins Dam came tumbling down in Vermont, the Edes Falls Dam departed the Crooked River in Maine, and the Kimball Brook Dam vanished from New Hampshire. Pennsylvania tore out 27 obsolete barriers that year, none taller than around 20 feet. Even the three-century-old Talbot Mills Dam that so vexed Thoreau may soon be taken down .

“We’re in this dam-removal renaissance, where we’re losing barriers faster than we’re putting them up for the first time in history,” says Nathan Furey , a fish biologist at the University of New Hampshire. Per one inventory , however, at least 35,000 dams still truncate northeastern fish runs, including more than 3,000 in Massachusetts, 5,000 in Connecticut and 9,000 in New York.

The $500 million project to remove four dams along the Klamath River in California and Oregon took place over a couple of years, with the river flowing freely by August 2024. The work opened 400 miles of salmon habitat, and thousands of the fish passed a former dam site in both 2024 and 2025.

Among the states destroying dams, albeit gradually, is New Hampshire, and one late-April morning I climbed into a car with Furey to tour a few of its newly free-flowing rivers. Furey had come to the Granite State in 2018 a neophyte to dam removal, having done most of his graduate research on relatively undeveloped Pacific salmon rivers in British Columbia. “But when you’re the fish guy at the University of New Hampshire, people want you to tell them what happens when a dam comes out,” he said as he navigated Durham’s leafy streets. “There’s a lot of people looking to you for answers.”

Furey’s domain is the Great Bay watershed , a tidal estuary fed by an arterial network of seven rivers. Historically, those waterways teemed with a roster of diadromous fishes: species that split their lives between freshwater and the ocean. That included Atlantic salmon, shad, sea lamprey, American eels, tomcod, sturgeon and, most numerous of all, alewives and bluebacks, a pair of silvery, foot-long fish collectively known as river herring . Sharks, striped bass, cod, seals, seabirds and other predators devoured river herring as they approached the estuary each spring, and juvenile Atlantic salmon may even have timed their departure from river to ocean to coincide with alewives’ return. While cormorants and otters gorged on alewives, young salmon slipped downstream undetected. There’s safety in numbers, and alewives supplied such prodigious numbers before they crashed that one historian deemed them “ passenger pigeons of the sea.”

Like their avian analogues, alewives fared dismally during North America’s colonization. Beginning in the 1600s, eastern colonists launched a dam-building spree , impounding and harnessing streams to spin waterwheels and power mills—gristmills for grinding corn, sawmills for hewing logs, paper mills for pulping wood, textile mills for spinning fabric. By the mid-1800s, more than 65,000 mills stapled eastern creeks, with catastrophic consequences. Over the past four centuries, scientists have calculated that New England’s dams have deprived its ecosystems of nearly 20 billion pounds of alewives—roughly the weight of 300,000 humpback whales.

To show me what happens when one of those fish-blocking walls comes down, Furey took me to the Bellamy River, its frothing course previously straddled by a sprawling brick compound, former headquarters of Sawyer Woolen Mills. The textile mill, long defunct, had been converted to apartments in the 1980s, but its two dams had lingered, funneling the Bellamy through a narrow, fish-stopping pipe. As they aged, the dams also became flood hazards, and in 2019 and 2020 a coalition of agencies, nonprofits and the apartment complex’s owner demolished them . Now the unfettered river churns beneath the brick colossus, ripping over a recontoured bottom of bouldery pools and pockets.

The dams are long gone, but can the herring navigate the obstacle course they left behind? “Alewives are not salmon—they can’t jump,” Furey explained over the Bellamy’s roar. “They’re not big, powerful swimmers like sturgeon ; they’re not eels that can climb and crawl.” After the dams came out, the state attempted to count returning alewives with visual surveys—in other words, by staring at the stream and tallying fish, an obviously imprecise method. “We have no idea how many fish come back here,” Furey said.

Furey had been tasked with answering that question. He and his students would capture alewives as they entered the Bellamy and implant them with trackers, including rice-grain-size microchips known as PIT tags, or passive integrated transponders, to figure out what percentage of returning herring managed to skitter through the rapids. We strolled past the apartment complex and upstream to watch Furey’s lab members set up the PIT tag reader that would register each fish. A metal box, containing batteries and a recorder, was chained to a tree near the bank; from it, a cable ran to a riffle, ready to log the serial number of any tagged alewife that wriggled past: a modern technology to surveil an ancient fish.

As Furey’s colleagues fiddled with the PIT tag array, they were observed with curiosity by the residents of the Sawyer Mills apartments, many of whom had taken their lunches outside to savor the balmy spring day. Whereas other wildlife migrations, like the trans-hemispheric flights of Arctic terns, unfold largely beyond human ken, New England’s diadromous fish often pass through neighborhoods and backyards. “They don’t need pristine environments—they can be right here ,” Furey said.

Many West Coast salmon runs collapsed within the span of human memory, but New England’s rivers have been plugged for so long that few residents know that they once ran silver with bluebacks, alewives and shad. “It’s a challenge to talk to people about these fish, because they don’t have any cultural memory,” Furey said. Fish depletion, therefore, is often a self-reinforcing cycle. The fewer fish there are, the less the public cares about them, a feedback loop the biologists John Waldman and Karin Limburg dubbed eco-social anomie .

Dam removal is often described as rewilding rivers, but it also liberates the human imagination. In a 2014 paper , the ecologist Loren McClenachan and colleagues published interviews with Mainers living along rivers where alewife runs had been restored, among them the Sebasticook, up which nearly two million herring swam immediately after a dam came out in 2008 . McClenachan’s subjects were jubilant: The return of herring had instilled pride, generated revenue from fishing and tourism, and solidified social bonds as kids and lobstermen gathered to watch fish ascend. If eco-social anomie describes a societal forgetting, dam removal achieves the opposite—a “collective remembering,” as McClenachan put it, that cures our amnesia and unshifts our baselines .

items.title: Bleached corals thrive within days when touching healthy neighbour
items.summary: https://archive.ph/zIPG4 Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50126253 Points: 21 # Comments: 0
items.content:
Scientists have rapidly restored bleached coral in a laboratory by placing it in contact with a healthy fragment, giving hope for reversing widespread coral decline.

Rising sea temperatures are stressing corals, causing the animals to expel the symbiotic algae that live in their tissues and give them their colour — a process known as bleaching. Because the photosynthetic algae (Symbiodiniaceae) provide corals with most of their nutrients, without them, the marine organisms are likely to starve and die.

A team of researchers has now shown that it is possible to fully reverse this bleaching process, in just days. It reported the findings in Science Advances on 14 October 1 .

“This incredible new result — that fast and full recovery is possible in bleached coral — can inspire solutions that eventually may be scalable,” says Fiorenza Micheli, a marine ecologist at Stanford University’s Center for Ocean Solutions in California and a co-author on the study.

In early 2025, marine scientist, and study co-author, Stephen Palumbi at Hopkins Marine Station in Pacific Grove, California, was working in the lab and noticed that two coral fragments in a tank were accidentally touching. Where the healthy and bleached fragment met, colour had begun to seep into the ghostly branch. “I’d never seen that before,” he remembers.

Danny Collins, who was studying how disease spreads through coral contact as part of his PhD at Stanford, set out to investigate whether algae can also spread and, if so, how.

He prepared ten pairs of coral fragments from the same animal ( Pocillopora damicornis )., Each pair had a bleached and a healthy fragment. He set up five pairs so that their fragments touched each other, and five with their fragments separated by a few millimetres. In the touching pairs, the bleached coral recovered within eight weeks.

“We were blown away when we watched the colour of the algal symbionts transfer over to the bleached coral, reviving it in a very short period of time,” Collins says. By week two, the symbiont population was doubling every four days, which is much faster than the recovery times seen in studies of coral recovering naturally in the wild 2 , 3 .

After touching the healthy fragment for a week, a bleached branch could fully recover on its own, even if separated from the healthy branch.

In the slightly separated pairs, the bleached fragments died after 20 weeks.

Using high-powered microscopy, the team showed that two coral fragments fuse together by creating a tissue bridge — enabling symbiont transfer. This only occurred for coral fragments taken from an individual of the same genetic make-up, called a genet. Fragments from different species and even different animals of the same species did not fuse together, and so did not nurse the bleached piece back to health.

Jones, R. J. & Yellowlees, D. Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 352 , 457–468 (1997).

items.title: Trial of German steakhouse heiress that sparked a huge spy scandal
items.summary: For 15 months, a high-security courtroom in Hamburg has been hearing the case of Christina Block, accused of ordering the abduction of her children.
items.content:
It is a trial that has gripped Germany, with a wealthy heiress in the dock for months and a case that triggered the country's biggest espionage scandal in recent history.

Christina Block, heir to a popular chain of steakhouses, is accused of ordering an Israeli security firm to carry out the violent abduction of her children from Denmark, following a bitter custody battle with her former husband.

There are allegedly connections with at least two former secret agents, from Germany and Israel.

In the latest twist, investigators in the case stumbled across evidence that has led to Germany's former intelligence chief, August Hanning, being arrested this month for treason and espionage.

Hanning's arrest stunned the intelligence community. Although his case has nothing to do with the Hamburg trial, he has denied allegations of involvement in an earlier attempted abduction of the children.

There was enormous media interest in Germany when Christina Block and six others went on trial in a high-security courtroom in Hamburg in July last year.

Block House restaurants, specialising in steak and baked potatoes, are a feature of many German towns. Their success over the past half century has helped make Christina Block's father Eugen a multimillionaire.

Prosecutors allege that she and a family lawyer, Andreas Costard, organised the forcible abduction of two of her children, who were staying with her former husband, Stephan Hensel, at his home in Denmark.

They say the operation was carried out by a 36-year-old Israeli citizen named only as Jonathan G and five others.

The abduction took place during the New Year celebrations of 2023-24, as the two children and their father were watching a firework display, according to the indictment.

Prosecutors say several men ambushed and beat up Stephan Hensel, and dragged the boy and the girl, then 10 and 13 years old, into a car.

On the approach to the border with Germany, they are alleged to have changed vehicles, taped up the children's mouths and tied the girl's hands.

The group are then said to have travelled on to Baden-Württemberg in a campervan. Prosecutors say the children were held there against their will until their mother arrived to pick them up on 2 January 2024 and took them to her home in Hamburg.

Christina Block, Andreas Costard and Jonathan G are charged with the abduction of minors, grievous bodily harm and unlawful detention.

Block's partner, a former TV sports presenter called Gerhard Delling, and three others are charged with aiding and abetting.

All of them deny wrongdoing, except for Jonathan G, who has admitted his involvement. However, he told the court he thought he was taking part in a rescue operation.

The trial comes after years of legal battles between Christina Block and her former husband, Stephan Hensel, over who had the right to look after the children.

Immediately after their separation, all four children lived with their mother in Hamburg. Hensel, who remarried, later moved to Denmark, where they regularly visited him.

In 2021, the two youngest children went to visit their father in Denmark, but then were not brought back to Hamburg as agreed.

A court in Hamburg ruled that Christina had custody and that the children should be returned. However, in February 2023, a Danish court ruled that, although the boy and the girl had been brought to Denmark unlawfully, they could not be taken back.

In May 2023, Hensel was charged with the abduction of minors, in a case which is still pending.

He has accused Christina of being violent with the children, charges she denies. She told the court Hensel wanted to take revenge on her.

She also denied knowing anything about plans for the abduction of the children from Denmark. Her defence argues that the Israeli security team had acted on its own initiative.

She told the court it was "a catastrophe" and that she had never wanted anything like that.

The head of the Israeli security team, David Barkay, who is not on trial but faces future legal proceedings, told the court that Christina Block and Costard had known about the planned repatriation operation.

Barkay, who was described by another witness as a former agent with Mossad, the Israeli secret service, said he had not shared all the details because he "didn't trust them."

The alleged connection with Germany's former spy chief, August Hanning, relates to accusations of an earlier attempt to abduct the children and bring them back from Denmark in 2022.

Prosecutors have said Hanning was responsible for arranging security staff sent to Denmark with Christina Block. His lawyer denies the accusations. Hanning has not been charged over the current Block court case.

However, while investigators were searching his home, they came across evidence to suggest Hanning was involved in buying some 2,000 documents from his former chief of staff and then passing on state secrets to foreign powers.

Which foreign power and who he is alleged to have given the secrets to is unspecified, but it has prompted widespread speculation.

Now 80, Hanning is in custody charged with treasonous espionage. His lawyer says he is being "unjustly persecuted" and that the charges are "unfounded".

Meanwhile the trial against Christina Block is currently on hold for two weeks - one of numerous delays and extensions over the course of the past 15 months.

The latest delay is because a witness, Stephan Hensel's new wife, failed to appear in court.

items.title: Guerra in Iran, le news. Coloni aggrediscono diplomatici europei a Taybeh, in Cisgiordania
items.summary: Axios: “Stop a raid Usa su Hormuz per evitare escalation prima delle midterm”. Unicef: “Dal cessate il fuoco a Gaza sono morti oltre 340 bambini”. Yemen: esercito, catturata squadra Houthi specializzata in droni. Wsj, 'Hezbollah chiede a Beirut restituzione esplosivo sequestrato'
items.content:
Le forze governative yemenite dichiarano di aver catturato una squadra di Houthi specializzata nel pilotaggio e nel controllo di droni nella provincia sud-occidentale di Taiz. Lo riporta Al Jazeera.In un comunicato pubblicato su Facebook, la 35 Brigata corazzata dell'esercito ha affermato che le sue truppe hanno arrestato la squadra sul fronte di al-Aqrud-Kahlan, a sud-est di Taiz.

Netanyahu: “Servono prove serie sull’attacco in Cisgiordania ai diplomatici”

Il ministro degli Esteri israeliano Sa’ar: “Condanno attacco a Taybeh, in contatto con gli ambasciatori dei Paesi coinvolti”

Usa: “Il 97% delle navi che tenta di attraversare Hormuz ci riesce”

Le Forze armate statunitensi hanno affermato che la "stragrande maggioranza" degli attacchi iraniani contro le navi nello Stretto di Hormuz non ha successo. Il portavoce del Comando Centrale degli Stati Uniti, Tim Hawkins, ha dichiarato a Fox News che il 97% delle imbarcazioni che ha tentato di attraversare lo Stretto di Hormuz "c'è riuscito senza essere colpito da un proiettile iraniano". "Le forze armate statunitensi hanno contribuito a fornire una protezione coordinata a migliaia di navi che hanno transitato in sicurezza", ha aggiunto. Hawkins ha definito "ingiustificati" gli attacchi del Corpo delle Guardie Rivoluzionarie Islamiche iraniane (Irgc) contro le navi, aggiungendo che "non stanno raggiungendo il loro obiettivo di chiudere lo Stretto di Hormuz".

Netanyahu: “Servono prove serie sull’attacco in Cisgiordania ai diplomatici”

Il premier israeliano Benjamin Netanyahu ha sollevato dubbi sulla responsabilità dei coloni nell'aggressione ai diplomatici europei a Taybeh , in Cisgiordania , denunciando "timori di una campagna coordinata, volta a screditare Israele e i residenti ebrei in Giudea e Samaria proprio durante il periodo della raccolta delle olive". "I filmati diffusi mostrano individui a volto coperto che affrontano un veicolo diplomatico. Altre immagini ritraggono un finestrino infranto e una persona a terra. Tali elementi, presi singolarmente, non chiariscono l'esatta dinamica degli eventi nè le responsabilità dei singoli individui. La vicenda è attualmente oggetto di indagine", ha sottolineato l'ufficio del premier.

Idf: “Uccisi a Gaza quattro terroristi di Hamas negli ultimi tre giorni”

Il portavoce dell'Idf riferisce di avere ucciso negli ultimi tre giorni, in raid distinti nella Striscia di Gaza, quattro terroristi di Hamas: sono Abd al-Jawad Juda; Ubaida Suhail Hamad Murtaja, Adham Khalil Mohammed Marouf e Mahmoud Khaled Mohammed Madhoun. "I terroristi promuoverano attacchi contro le truppe dell'Idf ed erano convolti nella riabilitazione delle capacità militari di Hamas", riporta l'Idf, secondo cui Marouf si era inoltre infiltrato in Israele durante l'attacco del 7 ottobre 2023.

Il Belgio condanna l’attacco ai diplomatici: ”Sanzioni ai coloni”

Il ministro degli Esteri belga Maxime Prevot ha condannato l'attacco di coloni a diplomatici europei a Taybeh, in Cisgiordania, sottolineando su X che "questa violenza è inseparabile dalla politica illegale degli insediamenti israeliani". "Il Belgio condanna l'espansione delle colonie e i tentativi di espellere con la forza i palestinesi dalle loro terre", ha aggiunto sottolineando che "continuerà a spingere affinchè l'Unione europea adotti sanzioni contro i responsabili di tali violenze e coloro che li sostengono". "In quanto potenza occupante, le autorità israeliane devono proteggere i palestinesi, garantire la sicurezza di diplomatici e giornalisti e assicurare i responsabili alla giustizia. L'impunità dei coloni violenti deve finire", ha affermato Prevot.

Il ministro degli Esteri israeliano Sa’ar: “Condanno attacco a Taybeh, in contatto con gli ambasciatori dei Paesi coinvolti”

"Condanno fermamente i gravi atti di violenza commessi da rivoltosi israeliani nell'area di Taybeh. Il ministero degli Esteri è in contatto con gli ambasciatori dei Paesi coinvolti, al fine di fornire assistenza alle forze dell'ordine nell'identificare gli aggressori e assicurarli alla giustizia". Lo scrive su X il ministro degli Esteri israeliano Gideon Sa’ar . "Senza sminuire la gravità dell'accaduto, è spiacevole che la visita non sia stata preventivamente coordinata con l'Idf. Tale coordinamento avrebbe potuto contribuire a garantire la sicurezza dei visitatori", ha aggiunto Sa’ar.

I strongly condemn the severe acts of violence by Israeli rioters in the area of Taybeh. A police investigation has been opened, and forensic investigators from the Judea and Samaria District are already at the scene collecting evidence. The Foreign Ministry is in contact with the ambassadors of the countries concerned in order to assist the law enforcement authorities, who are working to identify the attackers and bring them to justice. Without detracting from the severity of the incident, it is unfortunate that the visit was not coordinated with the IDF in advance. Such coordination could have helped safeguard the visitors’ security.

Cisgiordania, aggredito dai coloni un sindaco francese che partecipava al convoglio diplomatico

Coloni israeliani hanno attaccato oggi un convoglio di diplomatici europei che facevano una visita in Cisgiordania ed hanno aggredito un sindaco francese. Lo hanno dichiarato all'Afp un testimone e due diplomatici. C'è anche un video condiviso da uno dei diplomatici che mostra Bernand Baudoux, 78enne sindaco di sinistra di Aulnoue-Aymeries, nel nord della Francia, sdraiato per terra accanto alla macchina. Due diplomatici e un testimone locale hanno confermato la sua identità alla Afp . Uno dei diplomatici ha precisato che il sindaco non è in pericolo di vita.

Esercito israeliano: “La visita diplomatici a Taybeh non era coordinata, aperta un'indagine”

L'Idf "'condanna fermamente il grave atto di violenza avvenuto nell'area di Taybeh , nel corso del quale alcuni rappresentanti diplomatici sono stati aggrediti da rivoltosi israeliani". Secondo una nota del portavoce, la polizia e l'Idf sono in loco ora nell'ambito dell'indagine aperta. "La visita del consolato non era stata coordinata con l'esercito - sostiene l'Idf - e tale coordinamento è fondamentale per prevenire incidenti di questo tipo". "Secondo un accertamento preliminare, al momento dell'aggressione non erano presenti soldati sul posto. Tutte le circostanze legate all'episodio saranno oggetto di esame" aggiunge l'Idf.

Arabia Saudita: “Intercettati droni su Riad e altre regioni”

La difesa saudita ha riferito di aver intercettato quattro droni lanciati dai ribelli yemeniti Houthi su Riad e altre regioni del Regno wahabita. "Nelle ultime ore abbiamo intercettato e distrutto quattro droni nelle regioni di Riad, della Provincia Orientale e al sud", ha scritto su X Turki al-Malki, portavoce della coalizione a guida saudita che combatte contro i ribelli filo-iraniani.

Figlia della reporter del Washington Post aggredita in Cisgiordania: “I coloni le hanno quasi staccato un dito”

I coloni che hanno aggredito la fotoreporter del Washington Post, Heidi Levine, le hanno quasi staccato un dito. E' quanto denunciato dalla figlia Ashley Milner all' Associated Press , sottolineando che un dito della mano sinistra di sua madre è stato tagliato fino all'osso, tanto che un tendine era visibile ed era quasi completamente staccato dalla mano. La madre è stata sottoposta a un intervento chirurgico e ha riportato diverse lesioni, tra cui la frattura di costole e vertebre.

Coloni israeliani aggrediscono diplomatici europei a Taybeh in Cisgiordania

Coloni israeliani hanno attaccato un gruppo che comprende anche diplomatici europei nei pressi del villaggio palestinese di Taybeh, nei pressi di Ramallah. Sul posto sono presenti diplomatici belgi, polacchi e francesi, tra cui il console francese a Gerusalemme secondo quanto riportato dagli attivisti sul campo e dalla radio militare. I coloni mascherati e muniti di bastoni hanno lanciato pietre contro i veicoli diplomatici.

Il sostegno dell'Iran ha permesso agli Houthi di sferrare gli attacchi più potenti e sofisticati mai condotti finora contro l'Arabia Saudita e i suoi alleati yemeniti. Tale supporto include assistenza nell'individuazione degli obiettivi per attacchi con droni e missili, oltre a addestramento, intelligence e guida tattica. Lo riferiscono al Wall Street Journal fonti informate provenienti dall'Arabia Saudita e dall'alleanza yemenita che si oppone agli Houthi. Secondo le fonti l'aiuto avrebbe favorito un'offensiva che avrbebe portato a rapidi guadagni territoriali nello Yemen. Il gruppo militante controlla ora il tratto di costa che si affaccia sullo stretto di Bab el-Mandeb - un punto di passaggio cruciale per le esportazioni petrolifere saudite - e ha lanciato attacchi contro petroliere, infrastrutture energetiche e aeroporti sauditi; tra questi, un'azione che lo scorso fine settimana a Riad ha causato la morte di almeno 13 persone. Il contributo dell'Iran evidenzia la capacità di Teheran di sfruttare i propri legami con le milizie mediorientali, come gli Houthi, per intensificare la pressione nella regione. "Il legame è molto, molto forte a livello operativo", ha affermato Danny Citrinowicz, ex capo della sezione Iran presso l'intelligence della difesa israeliana. "L'Iran ha un interesse fondamentale nel successo degli Houthi: ciò danneggia l'Arabia Saudita e fa salire i prezzi del petrolio. Si tratta dunque di un interesse strategico condiviso, che non si basa su un rapporto di subordinazione tra cliente e protettore, bensì su una cooperazione strategica".

items.title: Guerra Ucraina - Russia. Trump sospende nuove sanzioni a Mosca. Cremlino esulta: “Momento storico”
items.summary: Il presidente Usa ha firmato un ordine esecutivo che revoca le misure approvate dal Congresso, il cosiddetto pacchetto Graham, che lui stesso aveva approvato solo un mese fa. Zelensky: “Incoraggia Putin ad attaccare”. Crosetto: “Errore grave limitare a Kiev accesso satelliti”. Zelensky ipotizza vertice a tre al G20 di dicembre
items.content:
Media, ordine per limitare uso di Starshield di Kiev è arrivato dalla Casa Bianca

Trump ferma importanti sanzioni e dazi del Graham Act sull'export della Russia

Trump, “Putin ascolterà il Papa per far finire la guerra? Credo anche lui lo voglia”

"Due droni sono stati intercettati e abbattuti pochi minuti fa dai piloti militari rumeni sopra il Mar Nero, pochi istanti dopo essere entrati illegalmente sul nostro territorio". Lo ha annunciato su Facebook il ministro della Difesa della Romania, Radu Miruta . "Il primo drone è entrato nello spazio aereo nazionale alle 17:59 ed è stato abbattuto in 2 minuti 25 km a sud-est di Sulina. Il secondo drone, nella stessa zona, è stato intercettato e abbattuto alle 18:05, 5 minuti dopo essere entrato nello spazio aereo nazionale, 20 km a est di Sulina", ha precisato il ministro nel post. "Nulla di ciò che abbiamo fatto finora è stato vano!", ha concluso il ministro nel suo post.

Zelensky: “Mosca vuol schierare missili balistici in Bielorussia per attaccarci”

Il presidente Volodymyr Zelensky ha dichiarato che i russi intendono dislocare in Bielorussia non solo postazioni di supporto per i droni, ma anche sistemi missilistici balistici, al fine di colpire l'Ucraina occidentale. Lo riporta Ukrainska Pravda . "Esiste il rischio di attacchi e di un'intensificazione delle offensive contro la parte occidentale del nostro Paese? Certamente. La Russia si sta preparando a questo? Credo di sì. Perché, a mio avviso, continuano a coinvolgere la Bielorussia? Sappiamo che stanno installando postazioni di supporto sul territorio bielorusso per utilizzare questo corridoio per i droni e intensificare i relativi attacchi", ha detto. "Ma questo non è sufficiente per loro: hanno bisogno del sostegno di Lukashenko per dispiegare altri tipi (di armamenti, ndr) sul territorio bielorusso, inclusi missili balistici. Senza dubbio, il dispiegamento di missili balistici in Bielorussia rappresenterebbe una minaccia, innanzitutto, per la parte occidentale del nostro Paese" ha aggiunto.

Zelensky: “I limiti a Starlink impediscono l’intercettazione di droni russi”

L'Ucraina non riesce a utilizzare i propri sistemi di intercettazione contro gli attacchi dei droni russi a causa delle limitazioni al servizio Internet satellitare Starlink. Lo ha dichiarato il presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky, come riporta Ntv, spiegando che il governo di Kiev sta discutendo il problema con i rappresentanti degli Stati Uniti. Secondo Zelensky, alle autorità ucraine è stato comunicato che le restrizioni sarebbero dovute a problemi tecnici. Tuttavia, durante alcuni test condotti sul territorio dell'Unione europea, il sistema avrebbe funzionato a velocità più elevate.

Un incontro trilaterale tra Ucraina, Stati Uniti e Russia potrebbe tenersi a dicembre, in occasione del vertice del G20 negli Stati Uniti. Lo ha dichiarato il presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky, precisando che il vertice potrebbe svolgersi anche in un Paese del Medioriente o in Europa, come riporta Ntv . Al momento, tuttavia, non è arrivata alcuna conferma né da Washington né da Mosca. Zelensky ha inoltre riferito che i negoziatori ucraini e statunitensi potrebbero incontrarsi già la prossima settimana. I rappresentanti di Kiev hanno discusso di questa possibilità venerdì con la delegazione americana. Il presidente ucraino ha infine sottolineato la necessità che anche l'Europa disponga di un proprio canale negoziale per i colloqui con la Russia.

Zelensky: “Ancora limiti a Starlink, è operazione pianificata”

Il servizio Starlink in Ucraina è limitato a 161 km/h, che rende impossibile utilizzare il sistema su intercettori contro i droni Shahed. L'ha detto Volodymyr Zelensky parlando coi giornalisti, riporta Ukrinform. "Oggi i nostri intercettori non funzionano per il limite di velocità. Il limite massimo attuale è di 161 km/h: superata la soglia, Starlink si disattiva e perdiamo il drone", ha detto. L'Ucraina ha inviato mezzi dotati di Starlink in paesi europei per test: hanno viaggiato a 180 km/h senza problemi. "Le restrizioni si applicano in Ucraina, ma non nei Paesi dell'Ue. In altre parole, si tratta di un'operazione pianificata".

Droni su Mosca, oltre 350 voli cancellati o in ritardo negli aeroporti

Oltre 350 voli sono stati cancellati o hanno subito ritardi negli aeroporti di Mosca a causa di un massiccio attacco di droni ucraini. Lo riferiscono i media locali, secondo quanto riportato dall'Associated Press. Il sindaco della capitale russa, Sergei Sobyanin, ha dichiarato che oltre 100 droni diretti verso Mosca sono stati abbattuti. Il traffico aereo è stato interrotto o limitato in risposta all'arrivo dei velivoli senza pilota. Secondo il ministero della Difesa russo, le forze di Mosca hanno abbattuto complessivamente 610 droni ucraini durante la notte, sopra 15 regioni della Russia, la penisola ucraina di Crimea annessa da Mosca e il Mar Nero.

Zelensky: “Pronti a negoziati ovunque e in qualsiasi formato, conta la pace”

"Siamo pronti ai negoziati ovunque e in qualsiasi formato: a tre, a due, a quattro, a cinque o più; non importa, ciò che conta è la pace. La prossima settimana c'è una possibilità, la parte americana ci ha dato un segnale, potremmo avere un incontro con loro". Lo ha detto il presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky rispondendo a una domanda del Corriere della Sera in una chat di giornalisti. "Per quanto riguarda i nostri incontri con la parte americana, come ho già detto, contiamo di incontrarci e siamo pronti a farlo in Ucraina, in Europa, dove preferiscono e come loro preferiscono. Se vogliono che sia negli Stati Uniti, che ci invitino e noi saremo pronti", ha aggiunto Zelensky mostrando ottimismo sul fatto che "la piattaforma americana funzionerà", nonostante Washington abbia sospeso delle sanzioni nei confronti della Russia. "Noi contiamo sul fatto che sarà esercitata maggiore pressione su Putin e non su di noi - ha sottolineato -. Altrimenti, sarebbe semplicemente ingiusto". Infine sulla posizione dell'Ue, il presidente ucraino ritiene "che sia assolutamente necessario che gli europei abbiano un proprio percorso e una propria direzione riguardo ai negoziati con la Russia". Zelensky ha infine annunciato che intende sentire il presidente turco Recep Tayyip Erdogan "sulla questione marittima e della sicurezza alimentare" nel Mar Nero, e i rappresentati dei Paesi del Medio Oriente. "Per loro non è facile in questo momento, hanno una guerra in corso. Non è una guerra su vasta scala come la nostra, ma hanno comunque le loro sfide. Tuttavia, li contatterò prossimamente", ha concluso.

Le sanzioni "stanno esercitando una pressione sull'economia russa, ma dobbiamo fare di più". Così il portavoce della commissione europea Thomas Reigner, in seguito alla decisione presa ieri dal presidente statunitense Donald Trump di sospendere temporaneamente l'attuazione di un ampio pacchetto di sanzioni contro la Russia. "L'Ue ha fornito all'Ucraina un totale di 230 miliardi di euro in aiuti. E abbiamo appena approvato il più ampio ampliamento del nostro elenco di sanzioni finora. Le nostre sanzioni stanno esercitando una pressione sull'economia russa. Ma dobbiamo fare di più", ha dichiarato Reigner, interpellato in merito alla sospensione delle sanzioni da parte degli Stati Uniti. Il portavoce ha inoltre ribadito quanto affermato venerdì dalla presidente della Commissione europea, Ursula von der Leyen, al termine di un incontro con i leader europei: l'Unione europea "non revocherà alcuna sanzione finchè la Russia non porrà fine alla guerra". La presidente della Commissione ha anche confermato che l'Unione continua a lavorare al suo ventiduesimo pacchetto di sanzioni contro la Russia. Parallelamente, nelle conclusioni adottate dopo l'incontro a Bruxelles, i leader degli Stati membri hanno espresso rammarico per "la decisione degli Stati Uniti di revocare temporaneamente le sanzioni sul diesel russo".

Il presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky ha dichiarato di ritenere che l'amministrazione statunitense rimuoverà ulteriori sanzioni contro la Russia, dopo che il presidente Donald Trump ha concesso deroghe ad alcune misure punitive nei confronti del Cremlino. "Purtroppo, la revoca delle sanzioni continuerà. Credo che l'accordo sul diesel sia solo il primo passo", ha affermato Zelensky ai giornalisti, riferendosi all'intesa raggiunta da Trump con il presidente Vladimir Putin per consentire alcune esportazioni di diesel russo, nonché all'annuncio della concessione di deroghe ad alcune sanzioni.

"Noi siamo dalla parte dell'Ucraina, non credo che si debbano fare troppi regali alla Russia". Lo ha dichiarato il ministro degli Esteri, Antonio Tajani, nel suo intervento al Convegno dei giovani di Confindustria a Capri.

Dmitriev dopo la rimozione delle sanzioni Usa: “Nemici della sicurezza globale non saranno felici"

"I nemici della sicurezza, della cooperazione e della sicurezza a livello globale non saranno felici". Così in un post su X, rilanciato dall'agenzia russa Tass, l'inviato speciale del Cremlino per gli investimenti esteri, Kirill Dmitriev, sul "proseguimento del dialogo economico tra Usa e Russia e degli sforzi di pace". Dmitriev aveva già commentato sui social "la sospensione del 'Graham Act' da parte dell'Amministrazione del presidente Trump" pochi giorni prima dell'entrata in vigore di sanzioni previste contro la Russia.

items.title: Helen Mirren si trasforma in una Patricia Highsmith da delitto
items.summary: L'attrice dà volto alla scrittrice in A talent for Murder, alla Festa di Roma
items.content: Una regina del noir e del thriller come Patricia Highsmith, diventa per una volta personaggio, in una versione tanto brillante quanto pericolosa, interpretata da Helen Mirren in Un talento per il crimine (A talent for murder) di Anton Corbjin, ispirato dalla piece Switzerland di Joanna Murray-Smith, autrice anche della sceneggiatura. Il film che ha debuttato un mese fa al Toronto Film Festival, è arrivato alla Festa del cinema di Roma e sarà in sala dal 26 novembre con Lucky Red, anche coproduttrice. Al centro della storia c'è il confronto che nasce tra l'anziana Highsmith ed Edward Ridgeway (Alden Ehrenreich), ambizioso e appassionato editor della casa editrice della scrittrice, arrivato da New York in Svizzera, dove lei risiede, con una missione precisa: convincerla a firmare un nuovo contratto e a scrivere un sesto libro sul suo personaggio più famoso, l'affascinante e sociopatico Tom Ripley, pronto a tutto (vari omicidi compresi) pur di ottenere quello che vuole: soldi e lusso in primis. L'obiettivo per Edward si rivela più complesso del previsto, di fronte a una Patricia, misantropa, sferzante, ironica, brillante, amante del bere, e appassionata di coltelli. L'autrice lo trascina nel suo mondo, rendendo sempre più labili i confini tra la personalità dell'editor, che in Svizzera inizia a frequentare la giovane ereditiera incontrata in treno, Clementine Balfour (Olivia Cooke) e quella di Ripley, in un continuo e pericoloso sovrapporsi di realtà e fantasia. "Quella che presentiamo noi, è un personaggio di finzione, basato fortemente su Patricia Highsmith" ha spiegato Mirren, assente a Roma, parlando del film, nel quale offre una nuova strepitosa prova interpretativa. Affrontare il ruolo per lei "è stata un'esperienza molto intensa, una delle più intense che abbia mai vissuto in un film". L'attrice premio Oscar sottolinea che Un talento per il delitto non va visto ne' come un documentario ne' come un docudrama su Patricia Highsmith: "Lei è un personaggio all'interno di una storia che è un mistero, un thriller, un'indagine psicologica, non dissimile dai suoi romanzi, una storia ovviamente molto ispirata alla sua scrittura. Non è affatto una rappresentazione letterale degli ultimi giorni della sua vita. È un viaggio nell'immaginazione." Per Joanna Murray-Smith era importante mettere in luce anche lo humour nero della scrittrice, nata nel 1921 e morta nel 1995, dopo una lunga malattia: "Quando la gente pensa a Patricia Highsmith, non crede sia 'divertente', ma in realtà era spiritosa e molto arguta. Era un personaggio molto dark, ma intelligente e brillante quindi c'è molto umorismo nel film. Questa è probabilmente la parte inaspettata dell'equazione, nel raccontarla" .

items.title: Il papa ha chiamato Putin per chiedergli una tregua umanitaria
items.summary: Mentre era ricoverato per la rimozione del tumore al polmone: ha chiesto di permettere il passaggio di cibo e farmaci a Oleshky
items.content:
Venerdì, mentre era ricoverato al Policlinico Gemelli dopo l’intervento di rimozione del tumore al polmone , papa Leone XIV ha telefonato al presidente russo Vladimir Putin per chiedere una tregua umanitaria a Oleshky, in Ucraina.

Oleshky si trova nella regione di Kherson: è stata occupata dai russi all’inizio dell’invasione, nel 2022, e da allora è iniziata una grave crisi umanitaria che si è aggravata sempre di più: in città non ci sono elettricità, cibo, carburante, farmaci e l’unico ospedale della città è pieno di persone che non possono essere curate o di cadaveri. È da maggio di quest’anno, quindi da cinque mesi, che non arrivano consegne di cibo e medicine.

Oltre a chiedere a Putin di consentire l’arrivo di cibo e medicine, papa Leone XIV ha chiesto di permettere l’evacuazione sicura dei civili: secondo le Nazioni Unite sono rimaste bloccate all’interno della città circa 1.700 persone (circa 2mila, dice il segretario di Stato vaticano, il cardinale Pietro Parolin), la maggior parte delle quali anziane e con disabilità.

Non è la prima telefonata tra papa Leone XIV e Putin: la prima era stata a giugno del 2025, meno di un mese dopo l’elezione del papa, che da subito si è esposto per chiedere la fine della guerra in Ucraina. Dopo la telefonata il regime di Putin ha diffuso una dichiarazione in cui ha detto di essere disponibile a «collaborare» per la tregua chiesta dal papa, senza aggiungere altro né dire in che modo.

items.title: What we learned from heated US midterm Senate debates
items.summary: As the 3 November election approaches and both parties fight for control of Congress, some clear themes have emerged.
items.content:
Candidates running for the US Senate in next month's midterm elections have taken to the debate stage over the past few weeks - with some heated exchanges and stinging personal attacks.

As the 3 November election approaches and parties fight for control of Congress, some clear themes have emerged, particularly within some of the hotly-contested Senate races.

Republicans running for office are facing the same question they have been asked in elections since 2016: how aligned are they with President Donald Trump?

Conservatives who have bucked the president in the past have generally not fared well with voters.

The president has seen low approval ratings in recent months, with polls suggesting voters are largely concerned with the cost of living and high fuel prices.

While some Republican candidates have remained in lockstep with Trump, a Reuters analysis indicated , external that two-thirds of candidates in competitive US House and Senate races have broken with the president in some way this election cycle.

Susan Collins, a Maine Republican running for her sixth term in the Senate who has repeatedly broken with Trump, is again putting clear distance between herself and the president.

"I voted with President Biden 91% of the time," Collins said during a debate last week.

"The fact is, this year alone, this Congress alone, I voted against President Trump 137 times," she said.

Collins is fighting a tighter Senate race than she expected against Democrat Troy Jackson, the former president of the Maine Senate. A New York Times/Siena University poll from mid-September suggests Collins could be ahead in that race by 3%, while others indicate Jackson is in the lead.

Elsewhere, some Republican candidates are choosing to separate themselves from the Trump administration's specific policy decisions, while expressing loyalty to Trump himself.

In Iowa, traditionally a Republican stronghold, Congresswoman Ashley Hinson is facing a tougher-than-expected challenge in her Senate race.

She is taking on Democrat Josh Turek, and some polls suggest he has a narrow lead.

Hinson has not gone as far as Maine's Collins in separating herself from Trump, but she has broken with the president on some policy points.

During a 13 October debate with Turek, Hinson was asked about the Trump administration striking a deal with Russia to import 300,000 tonnes to the US, followed by several other shipments.

The Republican candidate did not mince her words: "We need to lower gas prices in this country, we need to lower diesel prices, but I don't think we need to be making a deal with Russia to do it."

NEWSLETTER: Sign up for Anthony Zurcher's analysis in your inbox

As they have debated in recent weeks, the candidates haven't held back on deploying pointed personal attacks against their opponents.

The race for the vacant Michigan Senate seat - between rivals Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat, and Mike Rogers, a Republican - has seen its fair share.

Rogers, a Trump-backed former congressman, questioned during a debate whether anyone in his Muslim opponent's family might be on a "watchlist".

El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim member of the US Senate, pushed back strongly.

He called the Republican "a sock puppet for the Trump administration" and said he was "weak, cowardly [and] won't stand up until his poll numbers drop".

On Thursday, a protester interrupted the Maine debate and Collins suggested the disrupter was associated with her opponent.

Jackson hit back at Collins: "Oh shut up, I don't even know that kid."

Further south in Georgia, more personal attacks were exchanged between incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and congressman Mike Collins, a Trump-backed Republican.

What started as an exchange where Ossoff accused Collins of taking money out of Georgians' hands to give to data centre developers, quickly turned into a hurling of insults that included Ossoff calling Collins a "bigot" who has "hired half the Third Reich".

Incendiary posts on social media from Collins' son-in-law, David Alan Scheer II, have become a point of contention in the race.

In one post, Scheer blamed "Israel and Zionist Jews" for policies he said were intended to "undermine the white, Christian nature of America".

Collins defended himself by accusing Ossoff of "spewing" "craziness".

"I've condemned racism, antisemitism, hate; I don't care where the source is," the Republican said.

There are 35 Senate seats up for grabs this November, but in 21 there are no debates scheduled among the main candidates, an ABC News analysis found.

One race's lack of debates has surprised many observers: the Texas contest between James Talarico, a Democratic state representative, and Ken Paxton, a Republican and former state attorney general.

Polls in the typically Republican state suggest that Talarico could be in reach of a surprise win. Should he succeed, he could help give Democrats control of the US Senate by flipping one of the four seats they need to create a majority.

Talarico has accepted four debate invitations from different news networks. Paxton has not accepted any of those invitations.

In July, Paxton's campaign spokesperson told media outlets he would debate Talarico. But since then, the campaign and Paxton have said little on the matter.

Trump, who backed Paxton in the Republican primaries, has urged the candidates to debate.

"One thing about not showing up is you lose the opportunity to make the case for yourself, and instead, what you do is you give your opponent the ability and the opportunity to make your case as negative as possible," Peter Trumbore, a political science professor at Oakland University, told the BBC's US partner CBS News last month.

Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's weekly US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here . Those outside the UK can sign up here .

items.title: You could have invented transformers from memory
items.summary: https://twitter.com/heyyalexwang/status/2111158818730397932 Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50122878 Points: 436 # Comments: 103
items.content:
Large language models today can recall obscure facts from every corner of the world. Most recently, I was running late for a friend's board game night, so I asked Astra to remind me the rules to Dune: Imperium. It gladly narrated them to me as I drove over and helped me remember the rules well enough for me to play again. We're so used to asking models about anything that we take their vast knowledge for granted.

How do models remember so much information? And how much can they store?

In this post, I'll go through an intuitive way to look at linear maps, MLPs, and self-attention as different kinds of memory stores. From this intuition we can derive some heuristics for how much memory each layer can store.

The key property that characterizes a "good" memory store is its ability to recall what it stored. After all, even if we could store infinitely many facts, it's not very helpful if we can't recall them when we need to. The more memories we store, the more they interfere with each other when we try to recall one. So throughout the post we'll focus on one quantity, the interference-to-signal ratio, which measures how much the other memories get in the way during recall. The number of memories a store can hold before the interference grows as large as the signal is its capacity .

We'll develop this perspective and show how you can go from a linear layer to something better, an MLP, which improves both capacity and recall, and then all the way to self-attention, which has very good recall and can store a potentially unbounded number of memories. With 64-dimensional keys, that's a jump from about 64 memories, to about 2,700, to over a million.

Here are the terms we'll use throughout. A memory store is a function $f$ that holds $M$ memories, for $i = 1, \ldots, M$. A memory is one key-value pair: a key $k_i \in \reals^{d_k}$, used for lookup based on similarity, and a value $v_i \in \reals^{d_v}$, which is what we want to retrieve. To use $f$, we query it with an input $x$, and it recalls an output $f(x)$. A good memory store recalls $v_i$ when we query it with $k_i$, or with another vector similar to $k_i$. In the literature, a memory store that recalls by similarity is called an associative memory .

The most basic memory store is linear: it simply accumulates memories via outer products,

where the rows of $K \in \reals^{M\times d_k}$ and $V \in \reals^{M\times d_v}$ are the keys $k_i\transpose$ and the values $v_i\transpose$. 1

To store a new memory $(k, v)$, we simply add $vk\transpose$ to the existing weights. 2

Take a linear layer $y = Wx$ inside a network with a scalar loss $L$, and let $\bar y = \grad L(y)$ be the gradient of the loss with respect to the layer's output. The gradient with respect to $W$ is $\bar y x\transpose$, so a step with learning rate $\eta$ is

This recurrence is a memory update: it updates the weights with a new memory with key $x$ and value $-\eta\bar y$. For more on this view, see Irie, Csordás & Schmidhuber , who express a linear layer trained by gradient descent as attention over all of its training inputs.

To query the memory store with an input $x$, we multiply the input by the matrix:

So recall is a lookup by similarity to the stored keys: we compare the query with every key, and return the sum of the values weighted by those similarities.

So storing memories is easy: just keep adding outer products to the weights. But what happens when we try to recall one?

Let's assume for simplicity that every key is normalized to have length 1, i.e. $k_j\transpose k_j = 1$. Then

meaning we get back the value of the target memory , the one whose key we queried with, plus interference from every other memory whose key is similar to the query.

If the keys were all orthonormal, the interference would be zero and recall would be exact. But $\reals^{d_k}$ only has $d_k$ orthogonal directions, so we cannot get perfect recall once we store more memories than the key dimension: $M > d_k$.

What is the outer-product store's capacity? Here's an intuitive argument. There are $M-1$ interference terms. If the keys are random unit vectors, each similarity $k_i\transpose k_j$ is about $\pm 1/\sqrt{d_k}$. If the values are random too, with similar lengths, the $M-1$ interference terms add up like a random walk, so the interference's squared length is about $(M-1)/d_k$ times the signal's, and

once we store as many memories as the key dimension, the interference is as large as the signal, drowning it out.

Each bar below is one stored memory's weight in a single recall, relative to the target memory's weight (in red). Every bar adds a bit of its value to the recall. Drag $M$ past $d_k = 64$ to watch the small bars pile up until recall fails. The other buttons switch to memory stores we'll build later in the post.

Even below its capacity of about $d_k$ memories, the outer-product store produces significant interference during recall. 3 To raise the capacity, or recall more cleanly below it, we need to reduce interference .

The brute-force way is to make the key dimension $d_k$ larger, since a linear store's capacity grows with $d_k$. How large $d_k$ can be is governed by hardware constraints.

Alternatively, we can make algorithmic improvements. We can store memories more carefully: the outer-product store adds each memory without looking at the others, so it does nothing to cancel their interference. Or we can recall more selectively: every memory in a linear store contributes interference, even when its key has low similarity to the query, so we can improve recall by suppressing the less similar keys.

In the rest of the post, we'll see that storing outer product memories more carefully gives us the optimal linear memory store, which has about twice the capacity. Recalling selectively via nonlinearities gives us MLPs and self-attention.

The outer-product store writes each memory without regard to the others. Instead, we can choose the weights $W$ so that recall fits all of the stored memories at once. This is a linear regression problem: 4

When we store more memories than the key dimension, $M > d_k$, the least-squares solution is

This is the outer-product store $V\transpose K$ with one change: before we compare the query with the keys, we multiply it by $(K\transpose K)\inverse$, which undoes the keys' covariance $K\transpose K$. This whitens the keys, so the store no longer overweights directions that many keys share.

When $M \leq d_k$, the regression can fit every memory exactly, as long as the keys are linearly independent. So the optimal store recalls with no interference at all, even when the keys aren't orthogonal.

When $M > d_k$, we start to get interference, since there are only $d_k$ directions for the memory store to work with. For random keys and values, our interference-to-signal ratio becomes

so the optimal store's capacity is twice as large as before!

When $M \leq d_k$. If the keys are linearly independent, the $M\times M$ matrix of inner products between keys, $KK\transpose$, is invertible, and

fits every memory exactly. When $M no interference and we have perfect recall.

When $M > d_k$. Setting the gradient of the objective to zero gives $W K\transpose K = V\transpose K$, so $W = V\transpose K\,(K\transpose K)\inverse$. Both solutions are $W = V\transpose (K\transpose)\pinv$, where $A\pinv$ denotes the pseudoinverse of $A$: $(K\transpose)\pinv = (KK\transpose)\inverse K$ when the keys are linearly independent, and $(K\transpose)\pinv = K(K\transpose K)\inverse$ when they span $\reals^{d_k}$.

Now we can analyze the interference of $f(k_j) = V\transpose K\,(K\transpose K)\inverse k_j$. For a stored key $k_j$, the weight on each value $v_i$ is $k_i\transpose (K\transpose K)\inverse k_j$, which is exactly entry $(i, j)$ of the $M\times M$ matrix $P = K(K\transpose K)\inverse K\transpose$:

$P$ is the projection onto the column space of $K$, a $d_k$-dimensional subspace of $\reals^M$. Two facts about projections help us analyze the interference-to-signal ratio:

Compared to the outer-product store's $\sqrt{M/d_k}$, the $-1$ is the $d_k$ memories' worth of interference that the optimal store cancels.

We can check our predictions numerically. We randomly sample $M$ memories with unit-length keys in $d_k = 64$ dimensions, query the memory store with one of the stored keys, and measure the interference-to-signal ratio:

The outer-product store reaches its capacity at $M \approx d_k = 64$. The optimal store recalls exactly up to $M = d_k$. Past that, its interference rises from zero like $\sqrt{M/d_k - 1}$, and the store reaches its capacity near $M = 2d_k = 128$, as predicted. Since it cancels a fixed number of memories' worth of interference, the gap between the two stores shrinks as $M$ grows.

This optimal memory store is still linear in the similarities though. It must scale small and large similarities by the same factor. To do better, we need to change how the store recalls.

If we had a way to suppress the weight when $k_i\transpose x$ is small, then we can reduce the amount of interference from low similarity keys.

items.title: Perché sono tornato ad usare un computer con Windows On Arm e Snapdragon | VIDEO
items.summary: Abbiamo usato per due anni i nuovi computer con Snapdragon e Windows On Arm. Ora con l'AI hanno tantissimo senso, ma non sono per tutti.
items.content:
Due anni fa provavo il mio primo notebook con Snapdragon X Elite e il "nuovo" Windows on ARM. Ricordo bene il video in cui ve ne parlavo, pieno di critiche e di problemi dovuti ai limiti software di quel progetto. L'hardware sembrava incredibile. Windows e le sue applicazioni non erano lontanamente pronte a supportarlo a dovere.

Nei commenti molti utenti si lamentarono, dicendo che per navigare sul web e consultare documenti andava benissimo. Vero: cose che fa praticamente ogni notebook, anche usato, da 300 euro. Se sto spendendo però 1.699 euro di listino, come per quel Samsung Galaxy Book4 Edge, permettetemi di dire che desiderare anche un utilizzo "più pro" è legittimo.

Ho continuato a utilizzare quel portatile dal 2024 a oggi, e siamo quasi al 2027. Nel tempo la situazione è sì migliorata, ma non rivoluzionata. Tantissime applicazioni, anche creative, sono arrivate in modo nativo: la tanto discussa suite Adobe compresa. Il fatto che ora girino, però, non significa che siano perfette e funzionino a dovere. Capire poi cosa funziona e cosa no non è ancora facile.

Il medio gamma che accontenta tutti? Nothing Phone (3a), compralo al miglior prezzo da Aliexpress.com a 264 euro.
